newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea hopes for breakthrough with North at talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea hopes for breakthrough with North at talks.

text.p: South Korea hopes Red Cross talks with North Korea will lead to a breakthrough in inter-Korean ties despite the failure to produce agreement in the first such contacts in nearly five years, Seoul officials said on Tuesday.
Negotiators from the South Korean Red Cross were returning home from Beijing where they tried in vain to work out ways of speeding up food aid to the hungry North, they said.
"The government's position is to keep making efforts to promote dialogue with the North," said Lee Ho, South Korea's deputy unification minister.
"We hope contacts between Red Cross organisations will lead to more talks between South and North and serve to build up confidence in each other," Lee told Reuters.

Representatives from Red Cross organisations from the two Koreas met on Friday and Monday but their talks stalled over the exact amount and method of delivery for South Korean grain to the North, Red Cross officials said.

North Korea is sliding into famine after the Stalinist nation was hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996, with officials reporting deaths of children from malnutrition and farmers eating sawdust to fill out their diet.

Seoul officials noted that Red Cross contacts in 1984 arranged to discuss relief supplies after South Korea was hit by floods had opened an exchange of visits by art troupes, divided family members and government officials.
"It would be desirable if the success of 1984 Red Cross talks could be repeated this time round," a Seoul government official said, asking not to be identified.
"A lot of patience is required in any South-North dealings but we will keep trying," he said.

South Korean Red Cross official Park Hyong-joon said North Korean delegates agreed to resume dialogue through a telephone link-up in Panmunjom, the only crossing point in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) bisecting the Korean peninsula.
The South Korean Red Cross had wanted to set up channels for direct delivery of relief supplies. The North sought a promise of an exact aid amount before discussing procedures, Park said.

The South also wanted the grain to be moved directly between the two Korean organisations rather than using the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies as a go-between as in past shipments of aid, he said.

Northern negotiators said the talks would resume after the South decided on the amount of food aid it would give but Southern officials said the amount of assistance would depend on how much South Korean citizens were willing to donate.
South Korea's Red Cross is the only window for private food donations from the South to the North.
"The Northern side did not set a pre-condition for the resumption of talks," Park said.
Paek Yong-ho, secretary general of North Korea's Red Cross, said in Beijing: "I cannot say we are disappointed or we are satisfied because we're in the middle."
South Korea, the United States and Japan are scheduled to hold talks in Tokyo on Wednesday to discuss food shortages in the North and ways to encourage Pyongyang to join four-nation peace talks.
The peace talks, involving two Koreas, the United States and China, are aimed at securing a lasting peace on the peninsula locked in Cold War confrontation since the 1950-53 Korean War.
